extra.message: Password reset token returned in HTTP response — Complete account takeover by anyone who can intercept or view the reset token response. [verified: Same finding as idx[0]; the raw password reset token is returned in the HTTP response body (line 127: mock_email_token) and is displayed to the user in the React frontend (main.jsx line 108). The confirm endpoint accepts this exact token, enabling complete account takeover.]

Password Reset Token Leaked in HTTP Response — Attacker can trigger password reset for any known email and capture the raw reset token from the response, then use it to take over the victim's account with full access to all data and operations scoped to that user's role. [verified: The /api/auth/password-reset/request endpoint generates a raw token via secrets.token_urlsafe(32) and returns it directly in the response body as 'mock_email_token' (line 127). The confirm endpoint accepts this raw token directly via hash_secret(payload.token), enabling immediate account takeover by anyone who triggers a reset for a known email.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Authentication Endpoints — Brute-force password guessing, credential stuffing attacks, automated account creation spam, and password reset token brute-forcing are all possible due to unlimited request rates. [verified: No rate limiting, throttling, or brute-force protection exists on any authentication endpoint. A codebase-wide search for slowapi, rate_limit, limiter, throttle, or lockout returned zero matches, and no such middleware is registered in main.py.]

Session cookie missing Secure flag — Session token exposure via network sniffing; session hijacking. [verified: Same underlying issue as finding 0 — line 66 (not 64) sets `secure=False` with no compensating HSTS/CSRF/proxy control anywhere in the request pipeline. The session token can be intercepted over unencrypted HTTP, enabling account takeover.]

Session Cookie Missing Secure Flag — Session cookies transmitted over plain HTTP can be intercepted by network attackers, enabling session hijacking and full account takeover for any authenticated user. [verified: The `secure=False` on line 66 of security.py unconditionally disables the Secure flag on the session cookie. No HSTS middleware, CSRF tokens, or proxy-level Secure-flag override exists anywhere in the codebase, so the session token IS transmitted over plain HTTP on any non-TLS connection, enabling network-level session hijacking.]

Account Enumeration via Registration Endpoint — Attacker can enumerate registered user emails, facilitating targeted phishing, credential stuffing, and password reset attacks against known accounts. [verified: The /api/auth/register endpoint explicitly returns HTTP 409 with detail 'An account already exists for that email.' when a duplicate email is submitted (line 84-85), enabling straightforward email enumeration. The invite_code prefix check ('TENANT-') is a weak barrier since the prefix is predictable.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Password Reset Request — Resource exhaustion and denial of service via rapid-fire password reset requests, each creating database records and audit log entries. [verified: No rate-limiting middleware, decorator, or library (slowapi, etc.) exists anywhere in the codebase; the password-reset-request endpoint is unauthenticated and each request triggers DB writes (PasswordResetToken + AuditLog), enabling resource-exhaustion DoS.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Password Reset Confirm — Resource exhaustion via brute-force attempts on password reset confirmation endpoint. [verified: Same absence of rate-limiting controls throughout the app; the password-reset-confirm endpoint performs DB queries per request and lacks any throttling, allowing resource-exhaustion floods.]

CSV Formula Injection in spreadsheet exports — Arbitrary command execution when exported CSV files are opened in spreadsheet applications. [verified: Same CSV formula injection as finding 1, spanning export_rent_roll (line 45) and export_inspections. No sanitization of formula-trigger characters on any field written to CSV, and RegisterIn accepts formula-prefixed full_name values.]

CSV Formula Injection in Export Endpoints — When an administrator opens an exported CSV in a spreadsheet application, attacker-controlled formulas could execute commands, exfiltrate data, or perform other malicious actions in the context of the spreadsheet user. [verified: Export routes write DB-resident user full_name/email directly via csv.DictWriter with no prefixing of formula-trigger chars (=, +, -, @). RegisterIn schema (schemas.py:16) imposes no pattern restriction on full_name. Attacker registers with formula name, admin exports and opens in Excel → command execution.]

Unbounded file read into memory on CSV import — Server memory exhaustion and denial of service via large CSV upload. [verified: Identical unbounded read as finding 0 — import_tenants at line 172 calls file.file.read() with no size enforcement. The MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES limit used in store_upload() is never applied here, and no global upload-size middleware exists.]

Unbounded Memory Consumption in CSV Import — Denial of service via memory exhaustion on the application server by uploading an extremely large CSV file. [verified: The CSV import routes at reports.py:188 call file.file.read() on the full upload with zero size check. MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES config exists but is only enforced in store_upload() (files.py), not on these paths. No middleware limits request body size. Route requires ROLE_PROPERTY_ADMIN but that's auth, not a size control.]
